title: Why Doesn't the Bible Mention Boyfriends and Girlfriends?
paragraphs:
Why Doesn't the Bible Mention Boyfriends and Girlfriends?
The Question That Quietly Reveals Why So Many Christian Relationships End in Heartbreak—and the Ancient Biblical Truth That Still Changes Everything Today
You have probably noticed something surprising.
Open the Bible and search from Genesis to Revelation.
You will find husbands and wives.
You will find betrothal.
You will find covenants.
You will find fathers arranging marriages, promises being made before God, love stories, heartbreak, redemption, and lifelong commitment.
But you will never find the modern words "boyfriend" or "girlfriend."
Not once.
At first, that seems strange.

After all, dating dominates today's culture. Entire industries revolve around relationships. Movies, songs, television, social media, and even algorithms constantly tell us that finding "the one" is life's greatest pursuit.
Yet Scripture remains silent about one of the biggest parts of modern life.
Was God simply unaware that people would date?
Did the Bible forget to address one of the most emotionally powerful experiences humans ever face?
Or is something much deeper happening?
The answer reaches far beyond vocabulary.
It exposes the difference between a culture built around temporary feelings and a Kingdom built upon everlasting covenant.
That difference changes everything.
Because from the very beginning, God was never primarily interested in helping people find a boyfriend or girlfriend.
He was preparing hearts for covenant.
That single truth explains why Scripture seems silent.

The Bible was written in cultures where romantic relationships were understood very differently than today's dating culture. Instead of defining multiple relationship stages with labels like "seeing someone," "exclusive," "official," or "boyfriend," Scripture consistently speaks about relationships through the lens of family, covenant, purity, faithfulness, and marriage.
One Hebrew word beautifully captures this covenant perspective.
The word is בְּרִית (berit).
It means covenant.
Not merely an agreement.
Not merely romance.
Not merely emotion.
A covenant is a sacred, binding relationship established before God.
Throughout Scripture, God describes His relationship with His people as a covenant because covenant reflects His own faithful character.
Marriage becomes one earthly picture of that divine faithfulness.
This is why Genesis records the first marriage not as a romantic invention of humanity but as God's own design.
Genesis 2:24 says:
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."
The Hebrew phrase וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ (ve'davaq be'ishto) literally means "he shall cling to his wife."
The verb דָּבַק (dāvaq) means to cling, stick closely, remain joined, or hold tightly. It is the same word used elsewhere to describe Israel clinging faithfully to the Lord.
Marriage was never designed to be casual.
It reflects spiritual loyalty.
Centuries later, Jesus Himself reaffirmed this passage.
In Matthew 19:6, He declared:
"So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not redefine marriage.
He pointed everyone back to Genesis.
Back to God's original intention.
Back before culture complicated everything.
That does not mean Christians cannot spend time getting to know one another before marriage. Scripture actually encourages wisdom.
Proverbs repeatedly calls believers to seek understanding rather than impulsive decisions.
But the Bible consistently asks a different question than modern culture asks.
Modern culture asks:
"How happy does this relationship make me today?"
Scripture asks:
"Does this relationship glorify God?"
Those are not always the same question.
The New Testament introduces another powerful Greek word.
ἁγιασμός (hagiasmos).
It means sanctification, the lifelong process of being made holy.
Paul writes in 1 Thessalonians 4:3–4:
The Greek word for sexual immorality is πορνεία (porneia).
It encompasses every form of sexual activity outside God's design for marriage.
Notice that Paul does not merely prohibit sin.
He points believers toward holiness.
Christian relationships are not merely about avoiding wrongdoing.
They are about becoming more like Christ.
That changes how we approach dating.
Instead of asking,
"How close can we get without sinning?"
The better question becomes,
"How can we honor Christ together?"
That single shift transforms everything.
It changes conversations.
It changes boundaries.
It changes priorities.
It changes expectations.
It even changes heartbreak.
Many people carry wounds because relationships were built on feelings that eventually faded.
The Bible never teaches that feelings are evil.
Love certainly includes affection.
But biblical love always grows deeper than emotion.
Paul uses the Greek word ἀγάπη (agapē) in 1 Corinthians 13.
Unlike merely romantic attraction, agapē describes self-giving love rooted in God's own character.
Love becomes patient.
Kind.
Not self-seeking.
Not arrogant.
Not easily angered.
Not because emotions disappeared.
But because Christ reshaped the heart.
That is why Christian relationships are not ultimately about finding someone who completes you.
Only Christ completes the human soul.
Colossians 2:10 reminds believers:
"And you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority."
A boyfriend cannot save you.
A girlfriend cannot heal your deepest wounds.
Marriage itself cannot replace Jesus.
Only Christ redeems.
Only Christ restores.
Only Christ makes all things new.
That truth becomes even clearer when we understand another Greek word.
μετάνοια (metanoia).
Usually translated repentance.
Its deeper meaning is a transformed mind leading to a transformed life.
Many believers ask God to bless relationships that He first wants to reshape.
He invites us not merely into romance but into repentance.
Not because He wants to withhold joy.
Because He wants to protect it.
God is not anti-love.
He invented love.
God is not anti-romance.
He created marriage.
God is not anti-dating.
The Bible simply refuses to make dating the goal.
Holiness remains the goal.
Christ remains the center.
Marriage becomes one possible calling through which God is glorified.
This perspective explains why Scripture spends so much time talking about wisdom, character, faithfulness, purity, forgiveness, humility, patience, kindness, and self-control.
Those qualities matter far more than relationship status.
Because they prepare us to love like Christ.
Ephesians 5 gives perhaps the clearest picture.
Marriage becomes a living illustration of Christ's love for His Church.
Jesus did not pursue His Bride casually.
He gave Himself completely.
He sacrificed Himself willingly.
He remained faithful even when His Bride was unfaithful.
That is covenant.
That is grace.
That is the Gospel.
And that is why the Bible never needed the modern labels "boyfriend" and "girlfriend."
Scripture always aimed higher.
It points beyond temporary romance toward eternal redemption.
Maybe that truth challenges you.
Perhaps you have experienced broken relationships.
Perhaps someone promised forever and walked away.
Perhaps you carry regret.
Perhaps you wish you could erase parts of your story.
The Gospel says something astonishing.
Jesus specializes in rewriting stories.
The woman caught in adultery found mercy instead of condemnation.
Peter denied Christ three times and became a bold preacher of the Gospel.
Rahab's scandal became part of the Messiah's family line.
Paul the persecutor became Paul the apostle.
The cross itself transformed history's greatest injustice into history's greatest victory.
That is the Gospel.
Scandal became grace.
Death became life.
Sinners became sons and daughters.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If your relationship history is messy, your future is not beyond God's redemption.
If your heart has been shattered, Christ still heals.
If your past embarrasses you, grace still reaches farther.
No boyfriend.
No girlfriend.
No spouse.
No breakup.
No divorce.
No failure.
No regret.
No secret.
No sin is greater than the mercy revealed at Calvary when repentance and faith meet the risen Christ.
Perhaps today the most important relationship is not the one you are hoping to begin.
It is the One who has been calling your name all along.
Jesus Christ.

You never know whose life may be redirected toward Christ because you chose to make His truth visible. Sometimes evangelism begins with something as simple as sharing biblical truth that points someone to Jesus.

Share what spoke to your heart. Perhaps write, "Christ is still healing me," or "Jesus rewrites everything." Your testimony may become the encouragement another believer desperately needs today. They may be asking questions they have never voiced aloud.
Return to these truths whenever relationships become confusing, emotions become overwhelming, or your heart needs to remember that God's design is always wiser than our feelings.
Every purchase helps sustain this work while placing biblically faithful resources into more homes and hearts.
One surrendered heart has always mattered more to Heaven than a thousand perfect appearances.
